high.title: Peso May Stay Weak on Revived Middle East Conflict
high.summary: The Philippine peso closed Friday at P61.587/USD, a marginal 3.3-centavo gain versus Thursday's P61.62, but still posted a net weekly depreciation of 7.2 centavos versus the prior week's P61.515 close. The currency traded in a tight P61.555–P61.62 range, reflecting a lack of domestic catalysts and a broadly risk-off tone driven by the re-escalation of Middle East tensions. Analysts cited geopolitical uncertainty as the primary headwind keeping the peso on the back foot, with markets in a wait-and-see mode pending further conflict developments. For FX traders, the near-term bias remains to the downside for the peso absent a de-escalation in the Middle East or a materially dovish shift in Fed expectations. The P61.50–P61.62 band is the key range to monitor; a sustained breach above P61.65 could open the door to a test of P62.00. Watch for any BSP verbal or direct intervention signals if depreciation pressure intensifies.

high.title: Yields Mixed on Iran Conflict and Soft US Inflation Data
high.summary: Philippine government securities (GS) yields were mixed last week, rising an average of 7.4 basis points (bps) week-on-week at the secondary market per PHP Bloomberg Valuation Service (BVAL) reference rates as of July 17. The dual drivers were renewed Middle East tensions — which triggered a flight-to-safety and risk premium widening — and softer-than-expected US inflation data, which prompted traders to reprice Federal Reserve rate cut expectations more aggressively. These two forces created a tug-of-war across the yield curve: geopolitical risk pushed yields higher on the short-to-mid end as risk aversion spiked, while US disinflation signals provided some offset at the longer end via lower global rate expectations. For Philippine bond investors, the key watch items are: (1) the trajectory of the Middle East conflict and its impact on oil prices and domestic inflation, (2) the Fed's next move and its ripple effect on BSP policy space, and (3) domestic auction demand at this week's P90 billion Treasury offering. The mixed yield environment suggests positioning should remain cautious and duration-light until geopolitical clarity improves.

high.title: Government Debt Rates May Be Mixed as Treasury Increases Offer Volumes
high.summary: The Bureau of the Treasury (BTr) is offering up to P90 billion in short-term government securities this week, resuming cash management bills (CMBs) with P40 billion on offer — broken down into P20 billion in 35-day papers and P10–P20 billion in 63-day CMBs. The increased supply injection comes amid fresh market volatility stemming from the re-escalation of Middle East tensions, and analysts expect GS rates to end mixed as a result. The higher supply volume could put upward pressure on short-end yields if demand does not keep pace, particularly given the more cautious market backdrop. Bond investors should closely monitor bid-to-cover ratios at Monday's auction as a real-time gauge of market appetite and risk sentiment. A weaker-than-expected auction outcome could signal broader yield curve steepening risk in the near term.

high.title: BSP Securities Rate Inches Higher Amid Strong Investor Demand
high.summary: The BSP's 28-day bills were fully awarded at Friday's auction with tenders reaching P70.69 billion against a P40 billion offer, yielding a bid-to-cover ratio of 1.77x — lower than the prior week's 2.01x ratio (on P80.24 billion in bids) but still comfortably oversubscribed. The near-flat average rate with a slight upward tick suggests the short-end liquidity environment remains flush, though the declining bid-to-cover ratio may hint at marginally softening demand. For monetary policy watchers, continued strong oversubscription of BSP bills indicates ample system liquidity and that the BSP's open market operations are effectively mopping up excess peso liquidity. Any sustained decline in bid-to-cover ratios in coming weeks would be worth monitoring as a leading indicator of shifting liquidity conditions or evolving rate expectations.
